title: ⭐⭐ Practice: leaflets, either and the time that keeps running

questions.prompt: Rewrite this sentence using the word "either": "Neither Wassim nor his sister has visited the old town of El Kef." Which version keeps the same meaning and is correct English?

options.text: Wassim hasn't visited the old town of El Kef, and his sister hasn't either.
Wassim hasn't visited the old town of El Kef, and his sister hasn't too.
Wassim hasn't visited the old town of El Kef, and either his sister hasn't.
Wassim hasn't visited the old town of El Kef, and his sister hasn't neither.

questions.explanation: "Wassim hasn't visited the old town of El Kef, and his sister hasn't either." is the right rewrite: neither… nor… carries one negative for two people, so once you split it in two you have to negate both halves, and the second half ends with either. "Wassim hasn't visited the old town of El Kef, and his sister hasn't too." keeps too, which belongs to affirmative sentences only. "Wassim hasn't visited the old town of El Kef, and either his sister hasn't." puts either in front of the subject, whereas in this use it stands at the very end of the sentence. And "Wassim hasn't visited the old town of El Kef, and his sister hasn't neither." negates twice in the same clause, since hasn't and neither each carry their own negative.

questions.prompt: Read this extract from a leaflet handed out at a tourist office: "Three floors of glass cases take you from the first Punic streets of the town to the trams of the last century — coins, oil lamps, wedding contracts and letters. Our guides answer every question, and photography is free." Which of these four visitors should take this leaflet?

options.text: Mouna, who wants two days of sailing and windsurfing on the coast.
Hedi, who wants to know how the town grew over the centuries.
Nizar, who is looking for a quiet beach and a cheap little hotel.
Emna, who wants to buy silver jewellery at the lowest price.

questions.explanation: "Hedi, who wants to know how the town grew over the centuries." is the right visitor: everything the leaflet advertises is the history of one town told through its objects, from the Punic streets to the trams of the last century. "Mouna, who wants two days of sailing and windsurfing on the coast." needs a water sports centre, and the leaflet offers nothing outdoors. "Nizar, who is looking for a quiet beach and a cheap little hotel." needs accommodation, which the leaflet never mentions. And "Emna, who wants to buy silver jewellery at the lowest price." wants to buy, whereas the objects here are behind glass and no price is given for anything.

questions.prompt: Complete this sentence with the right pair of verb forms: "Mouna ___ photographs of the medina for two years, and she ___ more than three hundred of them so far."

options.text: has taken / has been taking
is taking / has been taking
has been taking / has taken
takes / has taken

questions.explanation: "has been taking / has taken" is the right pair: the first gap carries a length of time, for two years, and a length that is still running calls the present perfect progressive; the second gap carries a number of finished photographs, and a number calls the present perfect simple. "has taken / has been taking" swaps the two, and you cannot count three hundred photographs with a progressive form. "is taking / has been taking" opens with a present continuous, which describes this very moment and cannot stretch back two years. And "takes / has taken" opens with a present simple, which describes a habit and again does not reach back over two years.

questions.prompt: Read this small ad from a noticeboard in Sfax: "Group excursion to Ain Draham, Saturday 14 March. The coach leaves the school at 6 a.m. and is back at 9 p.m. 40 dinars, lunch included. Give your name to Mr Karray before Wednesday." Which piece of information does the ad NOT give?

options.text: The day the excursion takes place.
The price each student has to pay.
The number of places still free.
The time the coach leaves the school.

questions.explanation: "The number of places still free." is the missing one: the ad asks for names before Wednesday but never says how many seats are left, so a reader cannot know whether there is still room. "The day the excursion takes place." is written in full, Saturday 14 March. "The price each student has to pay." is there too, 40 dinars with lunch included. And "The time the coach leaves the school." is the first practical detail given, 6 a.m., with the return at 9 p.m.

questions.prompt: In the words of this lesson the strong beat does not always fall in the same place. Which of these four words is stressed on its SECOND syllable?

options.text: teammates
grateful
leaflet
career

questions.explanation: "career" is the odd one: you say ca-REER, with the beat on the second syllable, like hotel, police and machine — the small family of two-syllable nouns that break the usual rule. "teammates" is a compound noun, and a compound noun is always stressed on its first part: TEAM-mates. "grateful" ends in -ful, an ending that never takes the beat, so it is GRATE-ful. And "leaflet" is an ordinary two-syllable noun, and those keep the beat on the first syllable: LEAF-let.

questions.prompt: Which of these four lines is correctly punctuated and capitalised?

options.text: When we arrived in Tabarka, Mouna asked, 'Where is the tourist office?'
when we arrived in tabarka, Mouna asked, 'where is the tourist office?'
When we arrived in Tabarka Mouna asked, 'Where is the tourist office'?
When we arrived in tabarka, mouna asked, 'Where is the tourist office?'

questions.explanation: "When we arrived in Tabarka, Mouna asked, 'Where is the tourist office?'" is the correct line: a capital opens the sentence, the town and the girl keep the capitals that all proper nouns keep, a comma closes the opening clause, the quoted question opens with a capital, and the question mark stays inside the quotation marks because the question is the quoted words themselves. "when we arrived in tabarka, Mouna asked, 'where is the tourist office?'" drops three capitals at once — the first word, the name of the town and the first word of the quotation. "When we arrived in Tabarka Mouna asked, 'Where is the tourist office'?" forgets the comma after the opening clause and pushes the question mark outside the quotation marks, where it no longer belongs to anybody. And "When we arrived in tabarka, mouna asked, 'Where is the tourist office?'" leaves both the town and the girl in lower case.
